q: Fast pulse, fast breathing, cool pale clammy skin, blood pressure still okay. What is this?

opts.why: Epinephrine is still holding pressure. Heart rate and breathing are up. Skin is cool, pale, clammy.
Decompensated shock is when systolic pressure tanks and organs fail.
Cool pale clammy skin and a fast pulse are not adequate perfusion.
Cardiogenic is a type (pump/MI). These signs are a stage: compensated shock.

q: Compensatory moves fail and systolic blood pressure tanks. What is this?

opts.why: When compensation fails, systolic pressure drops and vital-organ perfusion fails.
Compensated shock still holds a near-normal pressure.
A falling systolic is not adequate perfusion.
Cardiogenic is a type (pump/MI). These signs are a stage: decompensated shock.

q: What adult systolic floor does this recap give for perfusion?

opts.why: Adult minimum systolic for perfusion is ≥ 90 mmHg. Nitro thinking uses 100.
78 is the 4-year-old example, not the adult floor.
70 is the constant in the pediatric formula, not the adult floor.
About 25 is a narrow pulse pressure, not the adult systolic floor.

q: What is the pediatric minimum systolic from this recap?

opts.why: Pedi minimum systolic is 2 × age (years) + 70. A 4-year-old is 78.
90 is the adult floor. Pedi is 2 × age + 70.
You multiply age by 2, then add 70.
25 is a narrow pulse-pressure cue, not the pedi add-on.

q: How do you get pulse pressure in this recap?

opts.why: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic. Under about 25 can mean worsening shock.
That reverses the subtraction. It is systolic minus diastolic.
You subtract, not add.
Pulse pressure is from the two blood-pressure numbers.

q: Dropping pressure, rising heart rate and breathing, cool pale clammy skin. What is this until proven otherwise?

opts.why: That four-part pattern is shock until proven otherwise. Then add extras to name the type.
Cardiogenic needs chest pain plus crackles on top of the classic shock pattern.
PE needs sudden dyspnea and oxygen that does not help, on top of shock.
Tamponade needs JVD and a narrowing pulse pressure or muffled tones too.

q: Breathing is adequate. What oxygen setup does this recap want in shock?

opts.why: Adequate rate and tidal volume → NRB at 10–15 L/min. Inadequate breathing → BVM with oxygen.
BVM is for inadequate breathing, not adequate rate and volume.
This recap’s shock oxygen is high-flow 10–15 L, not a 2 L cannula.
Give high-flow oxygen as part of universal shock care.

q: What position does this recap want for shock if they can tolerate it?

opts.why: Flat helps venous return and blood pressure unless they cannot tolerate it.
Upright is not the default shock position here. Supine is.
The recap says supine, not prone.
Standing does not help venous return in shock.

q: They are already hypotensive in shock. Nitro and CPAP?

opts.why: Nitro and CPAP both drop blood pressure. They are contraindicated if already hypotensive or in shock.
They drop pressure. You hold them in shock.
Nitro is also out if they are hypotensive.
CPAP is also out if systolic is already too low.

q: Shock plus crushing chest pain plus crackles. What type is this?

opts.why: A weak pump, usually a big MI. Left failure backs blood into the lungs.
Tamponade is JVD and a narrowing pulse pressure, not crackles from lung fluid.
Tension has absent breath sounds on one side, not crackles in both lungs.
PE is sudden dyspnea and a sat that will not rise. Crackles plus chest pain is cardiogenic.

q: Narrowing pulse pressure, jugular vein distension, muffled heart tones. What is this?

opts.why: Those three are Beck’s triad for cardiac tamponade: fluid squeezing the heart.
Tension is one-sided absent breath sounds, not muffled tones as the triad.
Cardiogenic extras are chest pain and crackles, not this triad.
PE is sudden dyspnea and oxygen that does not help, not Beck’s triad.

q: Chest trauma, shock, and JVD. Equal clear breath sounds. What type?

opts.why: Shared with tension: trauma, shock, JVD. Equal clear lungs point to tamponade.
Tension has absent breath sounds on one side.
Cardiogenic is a pump/MI pattern with crackles, not this trauma + JVD split.
PE is a medical clot, not chest trauma with JVD.

q: Chest trauma, shock, and JVD. Absent breath sounds on one side. What type?

opts.why: Trapped air collapses that lung and shoves the heart. One silent side is the split from tamponade.
Tamponade keeps equal breath sounds.
Cardiogenic extras are chest pain and crackles, not a silent hemithorax.
PE is medical sudden dyspnea, not trauma with one silent lung.

q: Sudden severe dyspnea, sharp chest pain, hypoxia that does not improve with oxygen. What type?

opts.why: A clot blocks lung arteries. Air in the alveoli with no blood under it will not pick up oxygen.
Tamponade is trauma, JVD, and a narrowing pulse pressure.
Tension is one-sided absent breath sounds after chest trauma.
Cardiogenic is chest pain plus crackles from lung backup, and oxygen still reaches blood.

q: Where does early shock pull blood away from, so the skin looks cool and pale?

opts.t: The skin and gut bed areas
opts.why: Sphincters close in less important beds. Skin goes cool and pale. Blood goes to brain, heart, lungs, and big muscle.
Brain and heart are where blood is sent, not where it is taken from.
Those are protected, not shut down.
Those hold baroreceptors. They are not the shunt-away beds.

q: Suspected big MI in cardiogenic shock. They can chew. Aspirin vs nitro?

opts.t: Aspirin yes; hold nitro if hypotensive
opts.why: Aspirin does not care about the pressure. Nitro is out if they are already in shock.

opts.t: Nitro yes; hold aspirin if hypotensive
opts.why: That swaps them. Nitro drops pressure. Aspirin does not.

opts.t: Hold both no matter the pressure
opts.why: Aspirin can still go for an MI if they can chew and have no allergy.

opts.t: Give both even if pressure has tanked
opts.why: Nitro is contraindicated once they are hypotensive.
